text_blocks.snippet: High blood pressure (hypertension) is officially diagnosed when your readings are consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg.
snippet_highlighted_words: consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg

text_blocks.snippet: Blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg) and uses two numbers: the systolic pressure (top number, measuring pressure when the heart beats) and the diastolic pressure (bottom number, measuring pressure when the heart rests between beats).
According to guidelines from the American Heart Association and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, blood pressure ranges are broken down as follows:

snippet_links.text: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

list.snippet: Normal: Less than 120 / less than 80 mm Hg
Stage 1 Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): 130–139 mm Hg (systolic) or 80–89 mm Hg (diastolic)
Stage 2 Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): 140 mm Hg or higher (systolic) or 90 mm Hg or higher (diastolic)
Severe Hypertension / Hypertensive Crisis: Higher than 180 mm Hg (systolic) and/or higher than 120 mm Hg (diastolic)

text_blocks.snippet: What to Do If Your Numbers Are High

list.snippet: Elevated or Stage 1: Focus on heart-healthy habits like regular exercise and a balanced diet. A doctor may discuss medication depending on your overall risk for heart disease or stroke.
Stage 2: Doctors typically recommend a combination of lifestyle changes and blood pressure medication.

Crisis (Above 180/120): Wait five minutes and retest. If your reading remains this high and you have no symptoms, contact your healthcare provider immediately. If it is above 180/120 and you experience symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, weakness, or vision changes, call 911 immediately.
